paragraphs: The oldest of all societies, and the only natural one, is the family. Even so, children remain attached to their father only as long as they need him to survive. As soon as that need ends, the natural bond dissolves. The children, released from the obedience they owed the father, and the father, released from the care he owed his children, all return equally to independence. If they stay united, they no longer do so naturally but voluntarily; and the family itself is then held together only by convention.

This common liberty results from the nature of man. His first law is to look after his own preservation, and his first cares are those he owes to himself. As soon as he reaches the age of reason, he is the only judge of the right means of preserving himself, and so becomes his own master.

The family, then, may be seen as the first model of political societies. The ruler is like the father, the people like the children; and since all are born free and equal, they give away their liberty only when it is to their own advantage. The one difference is this. In the family, the father’s love for his children pays him back for the care he gives them. In the State, the pleasure of commanding takes the place of that love, which the chief cannot feel for the many peoples under him.

Grotius denies that all human power is established for the benefit of the governed, and he cites slavery as an example. His usual method of reasoning is always to establish right by fact.[1] A more logical method would be possible, but none could be more favorable to tyrants.

According to Grotius, then, it is doubtful whether the human race belongs to a hundred men, or those hundred men belong to the human race; and throughout his book he seems to lean toward the first alternative, which is also the view of Hobbes. On this view, the human species is divided into so many herds of cattle, each with its ruler, who guards them in order to devour them.

A shepherd is of a nature superior to his flock; so, the argument runs, the shepherds of men, _i.e._ their rulers, are of a nature superior to the peoples under them. That, Philo tells us, was how the Emperor Caligula reasoned, and he concluded with equal justice either that kings were gods or that men were beasts.
Caligula’s reasoning matches that of Hobbes and Grotius. Aristotle had said it before any of them: men are not at all equal by nature; some are born for slavery and others to rule.

Aristotle was right, but he took the effect for the cause. Nothing is more certain than that a man born in slavery is born for slavery. Slaves lose everything in their chains, even the desire to escape them. They love their servitude, as the comrades of Ulysses loved being turned into beasts.[2] So if there are slaves by nature, it is because there were slaves against nature. Force made the first slaves, and their cowardice kept them slaves.

I have said nothing about King Adam, or Emperor Noah, the father of the three great monarchs who shared out the universe among them, like the children of Saturn, whom some scholars have taken them to be. I hope my moderation will earn me due thanks. After all, I am a direct descendant of one of these princes, perhaps of the eldest branch; for all I know, a check of the titles might prove me the legitimate king of the human race. Whatever the case, no one can doubt that Adam was sovereign of the world, as Robinson Crusoe was of his island, for as long as he was its only inhabitant. And this empire had one advantage: the monarch, secure on his throne, had no rebellions, wars or conspirators to fear.
